Coming from unmarked::occuFP()

Source: vignettes/unmarked.Rmd
unmarked.Rmd

The ‘unmarked’ package (Fiske & Chandler, 2011; Kellner et al., 2023) fits the false-positive occupancy models of Royle and Link (2006) and Miller et al. (2011) by maximum likelihood with occuFP(). crywolf fits the multiple-methods model of Miller et al. (2011) in a Bayesian framework. This article shows how data and formulas prepared for occuFP() translate to fp_data_wide() and fp_occu(), fits both to the same simulated data, and lists what differs between the two.

The data layout

occuFP() takes an unmarkedFrameOccuFP: one detection matrix y with sites in rows and all occasions in columns, plus a vector type with the number of occasions of each data type, in this order:

  1. occasions without false positives (the verified method);
  2. occasions with false positives (the automated method);
  3. occasions with certain and uncertain detections (detections coded 2 and 1).

The multiple-methods design uses types 1 and 2 only, so type = c(n_verified, n_automated, 0). crywolf keeps the two methods in separate matrices: fp_data_wide(y_auto, y_verified) takes the type-2 columns as y_auto and the type-1 columns as y_verified. Rows of NA in y_verified mark sites that were not verified, as in ‘unmarked’.

unmarked crywolf
y[, 1:n1] (type 1) y_verified
y[, n1 + 1:n2] (type 2) y_auto
siteCovs site_covs
obsCovs (automated occasions) obs_covs (named list of matrices)
type = c(n1, n2, 0) implied by the two matrices
type-3 data not supported

The same model fitted both ways

We simulate 300 sites with 10 automated occasions each, a third of them verified on three occasions, and a constant false-positive rate of 0.05.

library(crywolf)
sim <- simulate_fp(nsite = 300, nocc = 10, frac_verified = 0.3, nver = 3,
                   seed = 2026)

# site-by-occasion matrices, the layout of 'unmarked'
to_wide <- function(df, nsite, nocc) {
  m <- matrix(NA_integer_, nsite, nocc)
  m[cbind(df$site, df$occasion)] <- df$y
  m
}
y_auto <- to_wide(sim$data$auto, 300, 10)
y_ver <- to_wide(sim$data$verified, 300, 3)
x <- sim$data$sites$x

In occuFP(), true detection on both methods is described by detformula, so the two methods need an observation covariate that tells them apart. Here METH is "verified" on the type-1 columns and "auto" on the type-2 columns; "auto" comes first alphabetically and becomes the reference level.

library(unmarked)
meth <- matrix(rep(c("verified", "auto"), times = c(3, 10)),
               nrow = 300, ncol = 13, byrow = TRUE)
umf <- unmarkedFrameOccuFP(y = cbind(y_ver, y_auto),
                           siteCovs = data.frame(x = x),
                           obsCovs = list(METH = meth),
                           type = c(3, 10, 0))
#> Warning: obsCovs contains characters. Converting them to factors.
m_um <- occuFP(detformula = ~ METH, FPformula = ~ 1, stateformula = ~ x,
               data = umf)
m_um
#> 
#> Call:
#> occuFP(detformula = ~METH, FPformula = ~1, stateformula = ~x, 
#>     data = umf)
#> 
#> Occupancy (logit-scale):
#>             Estimate    SE     z  P(>|z|)
#> (Intercept)    0.156 0.125  1.25 2.12e-01
#> x             -0.766 0.139 -5.51 3.68e-08
#> 
#> Detection (logit-scale):
#>              Estimate     SE    z  P(>|z|)
#> (Intercept)     0.430 0.0526 8.17 3.12e-16
#> METHverified    0.234 0.1771 1.32 1.86e-01
#> 
#> false positive (logit-scale):
#>  Estimate    SE     z   P(>|z|)
#>     -2.99 0.131 -22.8 1.56e-115
#> 
#> AIC: 3266.285 
#> Number of sites: 300

In crywolf the verified method has its own detection probability, so no method covariate is needed:

d <- fp_data_wide(y_auto, y_ver, site_covs = data.frame(x = x))
m_cw <- fp_occu(d, occ = ~ x, fp = ~ 1, seed = 1)
#> Running MCMC with 4 parallel chains, with 1 thread(s) per chain...
#> 
#> Chain 4 finished in 28.9 seconds.
#> Chain 2 finished in 30.6 seconds.
#> Chain 3 finished in 31.6 seconds.
#> Chain 1 finished in 32.4 seconds.
#> 
#> All 4 chains finished successfully.
#> Mean chain execution time: 30.9 seconds.
#> Total execution time: 32.5 seconds.
coef(m_cw)
#>      occ_(Intercept)                occ_x      det_(Intercept) 
#>           0.15522435          -0.77425011           0.42786246 
#> verified_(Intercept)           p_verified              p11_ref 
#>           0.65954571           0.65820716           0.60529522 
#>       fp_(Intercept)               fp_gap              p10_ref 
#>          -2.98644676           3.41430922           0.04837542 
#>              p10_bar 
#>           0.04837542

Both fits recover the generating values (occupancy intercept 0, slope −0.8, true detection logit(0.6) = 0.41 for both methods, false positives logit(0.05) = −2.94), and with this much data the maximum-likelihood estimates and the posterior means nearly coincide:

Maximum-likelihood estimates from occuFP() and posterior means from fp_occu(), logit scale.
parameter truth unmarked crywolf
occupancy intercept 0.00 0.16 0.16
occupancy slope -0.80 -0.77 -0.77
true detection, automated (logit) 0.41 0.43 0.43
true detection, verified (logit) 0.41 0.66 0.66
false positive (logit) -2.94 -2.99 -2.99

Formulas

occuFP() fp_occu() Notes
stateformula occ site covariates
detformula det true detection of the automated method; site or observation covariates
(method term in detformula) verified_(Intercept) crywolf gives the verified method a constant detection probability
FPformula fp crywolf: site covariates only
Bformula none type-3 data only

Two differences in the parametrization matter when comparing output:

  • In crywolf the intercept of the false-positive rate is tied to the intercept of true detection by a positive gap, \gamma_0 = \alpha_0 - \Delta with \Delta > 0, so that at the reference values of the covariates a true detection is always more likely than a false positive. Without such a constraint the likelihood has a second mode in which the labels of occupied and unoccupied sites are swapped; an optimizer such as the one in occuFP() returns whichever mode it reaches from its starting values, so check that the estimated true-detection probability exceeds the false-positive one. Because the reference is where all covariates are zero, centre or standardize them before fitting with crywolf.
  • fp_occu() places priors on all parameters (fp_priors()), which matter little with as much data as above but keep the estimates finite in small or sparse datasets.

What crywolf adds

  • Posterior distributions of every parameter and of derived quantities such as the mean false-positive rate over sites (p10_bar), with convergence diagnostics.
  • A recorder random intercept on true detection (random_recorder = TRUE).
  • The observation-confirmation design of Chambert et al. (2015), in which detections on a subset of automated occasions are checked (fp_data(confirmed = )).
  • Cross-validation by leave-one-site-out LOO (loo()) in place of AIC, and posterior predictive checks (fp_ppc()).
  • Calibration checks by simulation (fp_calibrate(), fp_verification_curve()), which ask whether the model’s intervals are trustworthy for a given design and false-positive structure (vignette("calibration", package = "crywolf")).

‘unmarked’ is the better choice when you need type-3 data, false-positive covariates that vary by occasion, or a fast maximum-likelihood fit inside a larger workflow built on its other models.

Predictions

Predictions follow the same logic in both packages:

nd <- data.frame(x = c(-1, 0, 1))
predict(m_um, type = "state", newdata = nd)
#>   Predicted         SE     lower     upper
#> 1 0.7154715 0.03888113 0.6336171 0.7852370
#> 2 0.5388560 0.03097511 0.4778700 0.5987006
#> 3 0.3519150 0.04165223 0.2751642 0.4371623
predict(m_cw, newdata = nd, process = "occ")
#>    x  estimate     lower     upper
#> 1 -1 0.7153759 0.6353726 0.7862628
#> 2  0 0.5385834 0.4784579 0.5982293
#> 3  1 0.3510890 0.2735747 0.4330131
